pathway.title: VIASAT INC — Credit Snapshot
pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: 1. Viasat's total debt was USD 6,570.5 million at June 30, 2026, down from USD 7,204.3 million at March 31, 2025, and gross leverage is 4.58x with net leverage 3.37x on derived, unadjusted EBITDA of USD 1,435.6 million for the twelve months, against 5.70x gross and 4.43x net in FY2025. Evidence is the CP-1 metrics; the mechanism is lower debt plus a recovery from the impairment-depressed FY2025 base, and the implication is a better leverage position that is still above 4x gross and has stalled since March 2026 (net debt USD 4,838.3 million then and USD 4,834.7 million now). 2. Liquidity is large but not all permanent. Cash of USD 1,735.8 million exceeds current debt of USD 661.9 million, and undrawn revolvers add USD 1,150.3 million, but the Inmarsat revolver of USD 550.0 million matures on March 28, 2027 and the Viasat revolver of USD 647.5 million carries a springing maturity tied to other material debt, with conditions the filings do not describe. The implication is that dependable liquidity after early 2027 is closer to cash plus whatever is extended. 3. The 5.625% Senior Secured Notes of USD 600.0 million are in current debt at June 30, 2026, and the fiscal-year schedule places them between April and June 2027 by inference. The larger wall follows: USD 3,246.7 million falls in FY2030 and USD 1,341.3 million in FY2031. Refinancing access and cost matter because the Inmarsat term loan and notes carry effective or stated rates of about 9%. 4. Earnings are thin after capital intensity. Derived EBITDA covers cash interest 4.73x and interest expense 4.20x, but after capital expenditure of USD 1,013.7 million the remaining USD 421.9 million is only 1.39x cash interest of USD 303.7 million, and operating income of USD 108.8 million covers 0.32x of interest expense of USD 342.2 million. Depreciation of USD 1,014.5 million and amortization of USD 312.3 million carry the gap. The implication is that debt service relies on spending discipline and on new satellites adding revenue. 5. The reported cash flow flatters the run-rate. FY2026 operating cash flow of USD 1,589.9 million includes the Ligado lump sum of USD 420.0 million, leaving about USD 177.1 million of free cash flow for FY2026 and about USD 158.3 million for the twelve months, against reported USD 597.1 million and USD 578.3 million. FY2026 other income also includes the USD 168.1 million Navarino gain, which is outside derived EBITDA. A further USD 100 million Ligado payment remains outstanding with no collection date. 6. Business risk is moderate. Services are 71% of FY2026 revenue and firm backlog is USD 4,217.7 million, aviation services revenue rose in FY2026 and Q1 FY2027, and no commercial customer reaches 10% of revenue; against that, the U.S. Government is 16% of FY2026 revenue, the five largest contracts are 19%, product revenue fell in Q1 FY2027, and derived EBITDA for Q1 FY2027 was USD 361.3 million against USD 388.3 million a year earlier. Satellite execution risk is documented by the FY2024 ViaSat-3 F1 reflector issue, which led to a net loss of about USD 905.5 million after insurance receivables. 7. Structure and behaviour. Of the USD 6,570.5 million, USD 5,294.4 million is secured term debt, notes and the Ex-Im loan, USD 1,133.4 million is senior unsecured notes and USD 142.7 million is finance leases, split between a Viasat group and an Inmarsat group with separate collateral and guarantors. The documented behaviour is supportive for creditors: notes redeemed, an Inmarsat term loan repaid early, no dividends ever declared, no sponsor or controlling holder identified. Ownership shares, ratings and the May 2026 Cooperation Agreement terms are not supplied, so willingness is judged on actions only.

runs.text: Strengths. (1) Deleveraging: total debt is USD 633.8 million lower than at March 2025 and derived coverage of cash interest rose from 3.24x to 4.73x (Documentary Fact, CP-1 figures; the ratios are derived, so read as Analyst Interpretation of filed lines). (2) Liquidity: USD 2,886.1 million, with cash covering all USD 661.9 million of current debt and leaving USD 1,073.9 million after it (Documentary Fact). (3) Recurring services base and backlog: services are 71% of revenue, connectivity is billed in advance or monthly, and firm backlog is USD 4,217.7 million (Documentary Fact; the backlog excludes future recurring in-flight connectivity revenue, so visibility is understated). (4) Customer breadth: no commercial customer at 10% of revenue and the in-flight connectivity base of about 4,630 aircraft is growing (Documentary Fact). (5) Segment balance: defense and advanced technologies earned segment operating profit of USD 216.3 million in FY2026, steady with the prior year, beside a communication services swing to profit that mainly reflects the absence of the FY2025 EMEA impairment (Documentary Fact). (6) Creditor-supportive actions: debt repaid and no dividends (Documentary Fact for the actions; the inference that they signal willingness is Analyst Interpretation).

Weaknesses. (1) Near-term maturities and expiries: USD 600.0 million of secured notes by mid-2027, the Inmarsat revolver in March 2027 and the Viasat revolver springing date (Documentary Fact, with the notes' window an inference). (2) Capital intensity: capital expenditure of USD 992.8 million in FY2026 and free cash flow of negative USD 122.0 million in FY2025 (Documentary Fact); the dependence of cash generation on spending falling is Analyst Interpretation. (3) Thin earnings after depreciation: operating income of USD 108.8 million against interest expense of USD 342.2 million (Documentary Fact, derived ratio). (4) One-off support in FY2026: the Ligado lump sum and the Navarino gain (Documentary Fact). (5) Structure: two debt groups, secured debt ahead of USD 1,133.4 million of unsecured notes, floating-rate term loans of USD 2,542.5 million at effective rates between 8.86% and 9.38% (Documentary Fact). (6) Concentration: the U.S. Government at 16% and the five largest contracts at 19% (Documentary Fact), with termination-for-convenience rights described by management (Management Language, qualified). (7) Visibility gaps: no company-defined EBITDA, covenant levels or group-level financials (Insufficient Information; missing evidence is not read as adverse).

blocks.title: Transaction summary and new debt issues

runs.text: The principal transaction in the evidence is the Inmarsat acquisition, completed on May 30, 2023 and described by the company as the purchase of Connect Topco Limited, a private Guernsey company, "in exchange for approximately $550.7 million in cash and 46.36 million shares of our common stock" (10-K page:6). The 10-K states total consideration of about USD 2.7 billion, comprising USD 2.1 billion of fair value of the shares and USD 550.7 million in cash, with goodwill of USD 1.5 billion in communication services (10-K page:169-170) and USD 31.3 million of transaction costs in FY2024. The financing of that deal and of Inmarsat since then is visible in the debt record: the 2023 Term Loan Facility of USD 616.7 million was entered into at the closing (10-Q June 2026 page:33), the 7.500% Senior Notes due 2031 of USD 733.4 million were issued in September 2023 to replace a USD 733.4 million unsecured bridge facility (page:42), Inmarsat amended its facilities in March 2024 to establish a USD 1.3 billion Inmarsat Term Loan Facility and a USD 550.0 million revolver (page:34), and certain Inmarsat Holdings subsidiaries issued USD 1.975 billion of 9.000% Senior Secured Notes due 2029 in September 2024 (page:41), the proceeds of which, with cash, redeemed all of the remaining USD 1.97 billion of Inmarsat 2026 Notes (10-K page:181). Status of the transaction: completed, with the share issuance of about 46.36 million shares and a role rationalization of about 800 positions that management announced as complete in November 2023 and describes as intended to achieve operational and cost efficiencies (10-K page:110; Management Language).

New debt and debt events in the periods since FY2025, all completed: in May 2025 the remaining USD 442.6 million of 5.625% Senior Notes due 2025 were redeemed at par (10-Q June 2026 page:38); in November 2025 the USD 300.0 million Original Inmarsat Term Loan was repaid early (page:34); on January 21, 2026 Viasat and ViaSat Technologies Limited entered into a USD 188.7 million direct loan facility with the Export-Import Bank of the United States, fully drawn at USD 188.7 million at March 31, 2026, repayable in 16 semi-annual installments from May 2026 to November 25, 2033 (10-Q Dec 2025 page:56; 10-K page:178); the former Ex-Im facility was repaid at maturity on October 15, 2025 (10-K page:178). No new debt was issued in Q1 FY2027 and no financing is described after June 30, 2026 in the sources. The use of proceeds for the Ex-Im facility is financing of ViaSat-3 F1 launch and insurance costs and exposure fees.

Disposals and receipts that affect liquidity: the Link-16 tactical data link sale for about USD 1.96 billion in cash completed in January 2023 (discontinued operations, 10-K page:133); the energy services system integration business divested in December 2024 (10-K page:111); the Navarino UK sale agreed in December 2025 and completed in March 2026 for USD 203.0 million of proceeds and a gain of USD 168.1 million, to a subsidiary of ICG (10-K page:110, page:133); and the Ligado settlement, under which a USD 420 million lump sum was received in October 2025, USD 100 million remains outstanding "pending resolution of certain matters", and quarterly payments of about USD 16 million with a 3% annual escalator began on September 30, 2025 (10-Q June 2026 page:46). Of the lump sum, USD 267.5 million was recorded as deferred revenue and USD 152.5 million as interest income (10-Q Dec 2025 page:52). A subsequent event after fiscal year end: a Cooperation Agreement dated May 6, 2026 between Viasat and Carronade Capital Management, LP and the persons on its Schedule A is listed as an exhibit filed with a report dated May 7, 2026 (10-K page:124); its terms, purpose and any board or governance changes are Not supplied. No merger, tender, spin-off, refinancing or sponsor transaction is described after June 30, 2026 in any source.

fields.value: Viasat has deleveraged and improved cover over the past year, but a refinancing event sits close and the headline numbers flatter the run-rate. On the derived basis stated below, total debt to EBITDA is 4.58x for LTM June 2026 against 5.70x for FY2025 and 4.50x for FY2026, and net debt to EBITDA is 3.37x against 4.43x and 3.31x. LTM is slightly worse than FY2026 because the Q1 FY2027 EBITDA is lower than the Q1 FY2026 quarter it replaces while debt fell by only USD 14.6 million between March and June 2026. Gross debt was USD 6,570.5 million at June 30, 2026, of which USD 661.9 million is current, including the USD 600.0 million 5.625% senior secured notes due 2027. Liquidity is USD 1,735.8 million of cash plus USD 1,150.3 million of undrawn revolver availability, but the Inmarsat USD 550.0 million revolver matures on March 28, 2027 and the Viasat revolver carries a springing maturity tied to other material debt. The strongest support is the cash balance, which covers the whole current debt balance, and the 4.73x LTM coverage of cash interest. The weakest point is quality of the base: FY2026 cash flow from operations includes the USD 420.0 million Ligado lump sum and FY2026 other income includes a USD 168.1 million gain on the Navarino sale, and the company prints no EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA or covenant ratio. What decides the outcome is the 2027 refinancing, the terms of the Viasat revolver springing maturity (conditions not described in the sources), and whether the ViaSat-3 satellites in service lift earnings while capital spending of about USD 1.0 billion a year continues. fields.value: Viasat, Inc. is a Delaware-incorporated global satellite communications and defense technology company with two segments and no financial sponsor or parent named in the pack. Communication services (FY2026 revenue USD 3,299.7 million) sells aviation, government satcom, maritime and fixed broadband connectivity from an owned fleet of 23 in-service or operational satellites; defense and advanced technologies (USD 1,340.6 million) sells encryption, tactical networking and space systems to governments. For a creditor the business is recurring in services, which are 71% of FY2026 revenue, but its cash needs are driven by roughly USD 1.0 billion a year of capital spending and by satellite programs that have already cost it: the ViaSat-3 F1 reflector issue left less than 10% of throughput recovered and led to a net loss of about USD 905.5 million in FY2024. The defining transaction is the May 2023 Inmarsat acquisition for about USD 2.7 billion of consideration, which created a second, separately financed debt group; in the last two fiscal years the documented actions are repayment (the 2025 Notes redeemed in May 2025, the Original Inmarsat Term Loan repaid early in November 2025, total debt down from USD 7,204.3 million to USD 6,570.5 million) and asset sales (the Navarino UK interest for USD 203.0 million in March 2026), with no dividend ever declared. Strongest support: diversified commercial customers, a firm backlog of USD 4,217.7 million at June 30, 2026, and the in-flight connectivity base of about 4,630 aircraft. Weakest points: concentration in the U.S. Government at 16% of FY2026 revenue and five contracts at 19%, the incomplete ownership picture, and the 2027 refinancing. What decides the outcome is whether ViaSat-3 F2 and F3 reach commercial service as expected and lift revenue while spending falls, and how the 2027 Notes and the Inmarsat revolver expiring in March 2027 are handled. The pack ends at June 30, 2026, so whether the satellites entered service on the expected dates is not evidenced. Ownership, control rights and sponsor behaviour cannot be judged beyond the facts below because the proxy statement is not in the pack.

fields.value: The principal transaction in the evidence is the Inmarsat acquisition, completed on May 30, 2023 and described by the company as the purchase of Connect Topco Limited, a private Guernsey company, "in exchange for approximately $550.7 million in cash and 46.36 million shares of our common stock" (10-K page:6). The 10-K states total consideration of about USD 2.7 billion, comprising USD 2.1 billion of fair value of the shares and USD 550.7 million in cash, with goodwill of USD 1.5 billion in communication services (10-K page:169-170) and USD 31.3 million of transaction costs in FY2024. The financing of that deal and of Inmarsat since then is visible in the debt record: the 2023 Term Loan Facility of USD 616.7 million was entered into at the closing (10-Q June 2026 page:33), the 7.500% Senior Notes due 2031 of USD 733.4 million were issued in September 2023 to replace a USD 733.4 million unsecured bridge facility (page:42), Inmarsat amended its facilities in March 2024 to establish a USD 1.3 billion Inmarsat Term Loan Facility and a USD 550.0 million revolver (page:34), and certain Inmarsat Holdings subsidiaries issued USD 1.975 billion of 9.000% Senior Secured Notes due 2029 in September 2024 (page:41), the proceeds of which, with cash, redeemed all of the remaining USD 1.97 billion of Inmarsat 2026 Notes (10-K page:181). Status of the transaction: completed, with the share issuance of about 46.36 million shares and a role rationalization of about 800 positions that management announced as complete in November 2023 and describes as intended to achieve operational and cost efficiencies (10-K page:110; Management Language).

The use of proceeds for the Ex-Im facility is financing of ViaSat-3 F1 launch and insurance costs and exposure fees.

fields.value: 1. Revenue durability. Evidence: services were 71% of FY2026 revenue, connectivity contracts require "advance or recurring monthly payments" (10-Q June 2026 page:6), firm backlog stood at USD 4,217.7 million, and aviation services revenue rose from USD 1,048,225 thousand to USD 1,191,426 thousand in FY2026 (10-K page:205). Risk mechanic: recurring service billing and a growing in-flight connectivity base (about 4,630 aircraft) support revenue visibility and cash conversion, but fixed services revenue fell from USD 741,601 thousand to USD 607,693 thousand as bandwidth was reallocated to aviation (10-K page:106), so growth depends on a shrinking consumer line being replaced. Credit implication: supports debt service capacity and refinancing access, tempered by capacity constraints before new satellites enter service; the backlog excludes future recurring IFC revenue (10-K page:108), so it understates aviation visibility. The Q1 FY2027 revenue decline (product revenues fell) is a counter-signal, small in size.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 2. Margin and cash-flow risk. Evidence: capital expenditure of USD 992,774 thousand in FY2026, a USD 169.4 million impairment and other liabilities for the EMEA exit in FY2025, and in FY2024 a reduction of about USD 1.67 billion in the carrying value of satellites under construction, partly offset by about USD 770.0 million of insurance claim receivables (10-K page:137). Risk mechanic: owned-satellite capital intensity and launch or anomaly risk absorb cash flow ahead of revenue, and management itself expects higher operating costs before new satellites reach commercial service (10-Q June 2026 page:74). Credit implication: free cash flow depends on capital spending falling as satellites complete; FY2026 cash flow also benefited from the Ligado lump sum and the Navarino proceeds (CP-1), so run-rate debt service coverage is weaker than the headline. The ViaSat-3 F1 reflector issue is the documented precedent for execution risk.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 3. Concentration risk. Evidence: U.S. Government 16% of FY2026 revenue and five largest contracts 19%; "A majority of our contracts can be terminated at the convenience of the customer" (10-Q June 2026 page:69); DCAA is auditing fiscal 2025 incurred costs (page:9). Risk mechanic: government funding delays, audits and termination rights can interrupt cash receipts and revise revenue; a USD 15.1 million reserve exists for refunds. Credit implication: moderate concentration that matters most in a downturn or shutdown; no single commercial customer reaches 10%.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 4. Sponsor alignment. Evidence: no sponsor, no dividends, repayment actions, no distributions beyond TrellisWare's minority. Risk mechanic: absent a controlling owner with a distribution incentive, leakage risk to creditors is low on documented actions, but ownership concentration and board rights are Not disclosed. Credit implication: alignment appears neutral to supportive on documented actions only; willingness is not inferred from identity. Counter-evidence: the Cooperation Agreement of May 2026 is unexplained and could alter board composition; its terms are Not supplied.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 5. Structure and key uncertainties. Evidence: two debt groups with separate collateral and guarantors (CP-1), the Inmarsat revolver maturing March 28, 2027, the 2027 Notes in current debt, and a Viasat revolver with a springing maturity. Risk mechanic: creditor claims are structurally separated, so group-level cash and leverage drive recoveries and refinancing choices, and the springing date can remove revolver availability early. Credit implication: refinancing timing and group-level disclosure are the key uncertainties; recovery prospects cannot be assessed beyond noting the liens described, and no recovery conclusion is made.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Viasat's credit is adequate but exposed: debt has fallen and liquidity is ample, yet a USD 600.0 million secured-note maturity falls due by mid-2027 and cash generation depends on satellite spending easing. The strongest support is liquidity of USD 2,886.1 million and a recurring services base, with gross leverage down to 4.58x on derived EBITDA for the twelve months to June 2026 from 5.70x in FY2025. The weakest point is thin earnings after spending: derived EBITDA less capital expenditure was only 1.39x cash interest, and operating income covers just 0.32x of interest expense. What decides the outcome is whether the ViaSat-3 satellites lift revenue while capital spending of about USD 1.0 billion a year falls, and how the 2027 Notes and the Inmarsat revolver are refinanced.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 1. Viasat's total debt was USD 6,570.5 million at June 30, 2026, down from USD 7,204.3 million at March 31, 2025, and gross leverage is 4.58x with net leverage 3.37x on derived, unadjusted EBITDA of USD 1,435.6 million for the twelve months, against 5.70x gross and 4.43x net in FY2025. Evidence is the CP-1 metrics; the mechanism is lower debt plus a recovery from the impairment-depressed FY2025 base, and the implication is a better leverage position that is still above 4x gross and has stalled since March 2026 (net debt USD 4,838.3 million then and USD 4,834.7 million now).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 2. Liquidity is large but not all permanent. Cash of USD 1,735.8 million exceeds current debt of USD 661.9 million, and undrawn revolvers add USD 1,150.3 million, but the Inmarsat revolver of USD 550.0 million matures on March 28, 2027 and the Viasat revolver of USD 647.5 million carries a springing maturity tied to other material debt, with conditions the filings do not describe. The implication is that dependable liquidity after early 2027 is closer to cash plus whatever is extended.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 3. The 5.625% Senior Secured Notes of USD 600.0 million are in current debt at June 30, 2026, and the fiscal-year schedule places them between April and June 2027 by inference. The larger wall follows: USD 3,246.7 million falls in FY2030 and USD 1,341.3 million in FY2031. Refinancing access and cost matter because the Inmarsat term loan and notes carry effective or stated rates of about 9%.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 4. Earnings are thin after capital intensity. Derived EBITDA covers cash interest 4.73x and interest expense 4.20x, but after capital expenditure of USD 1,013.7 million the remaining USD 421.9 million is only 1.39x cash interest of USD 303.7 million, and operating income of USD 108.8 million covers 0.32x of interest expense of USD 342.2 million. Depreciation of USD 1,014.5 million and amortization of USD 312.3 million carry the gap. The implication is that debt service relies on spending discipline and on new satellites adding revenue.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 5. The reported cash flow flatters the run-rate. FY2026 operating cash flow of USD 1,589.9 million includes the Ligado lump sum of USD 420.0 million, leaving about USD 177.1 million of free cash flow for FY2026 and about USD 158.3 million for the twelve months, against reported USD 597.1 million and USD 578.3 million. FY2026 other income also includes the USD 168.1 million Navarino gain, which is outside derived EBITDA. A further USD 100 million Ligado payment remains outstanding with no collection date.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 6. Business risk is moderate. Services are 71% of FY2026 revenue and firm backlog is USD 4,217.7 million, aviation services revenue rose in FY2026 and Q1 FY2027, and no commercial customer reaches 10% of revenue; against that, the U.S. Government is 16% of FY2026 revenue, the five largest contracts are 19%, product revenue fell in Q1 FY2027, and derived EBITDA for Q1 FY2027 was USD 361.3 million against USD 388.3 million a year earlier. Satellite execution risk is documented by the FY2024 ViaSat-3 F1 reflector issue, which led to a net loss of about USD 905.5 million after insurance receivables.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 7. Structure and behaviour. Of the USD 6,570.5 million, USD 5,294.4 million is secured term debt, notes and the Ex-Im loan, USD 1,133.4 million is senior unsecured notes and USD 142.7 million is finance leases, split between a Viasat group and an Inmarsat group with separate collateral and guarantors. The documented behaviour is supportive for creditors: notes redeemed, an Inmarsat term loan repaid early, no dividends ever declared, no sponsor or controlling holder identified. Ownership shares, ratings and the May 2026 Cooperation Agreement terms are not supplied, so willingness is judged on actions only.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Strengths. (1) Deleveraging: total debt is USD 633.8 million lower than at March 2025 and derived coverage of cash interest rose from 3.24x to 4.73x (Documentary Fact, CP-1 figures; the ratios are derived, so read as Analyst Interpretation of filed lines). (2) Liquidity: USD 2,886.1 million, with cash covering all USD 661.9 million of current debt and leaving USD 1,073.9 million after it (Documentary Fact). (3) Recurring services base and backlog: services are 71% of revenue, connectivity is billed in advance or monthly, and firm backlog is USD 4,217.7 million (Documentary Fact; the backlog excludes future recurring in-flight connectivity revenue, so visibility is understated). (4) Customer breadth: no commercial customer at 10% of revenue and the in-flight connectivity base of about 4,630 aircraft is growing (Documentary Fact). (5) Segment balance: defense and advanced technologies earned segment operating profit of USD 216.3 million in FY2026, steady with the prior year, beside a communication services swing to profit that mainly reflects the absence of the FY2025 EMEA impairment (Documentary Fact). (6) Creditor-supportive actions: debt repaid and no dividends (Documentary Fact for the actions; the inference that they signal willingness is Analyst Interpretation).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Weaknesses. (1) Near-term maturities and expiries: USD 600.0 million of secured notes by mid-2027, the Inmarsat revolver in March 2027 and the Viasat revolver springing date (Documentary Fact, with the notes' window an inference). (2) Capital intensity: capital expenditure of USD 992.8 million in FY2026 and free cash flow of negative USD 122.0 million in FY2025 (Documentary Fact); the dependence of cash generation on spending falling is Analyst Interpretation. (3) Thin earnings after depreciation: operating income of USD 108.8 million against interest expense of USD 342.2 million (Documentary Fact, derived ratio). (4) One-off support in FY2026: the Ligado lump sum and the Navarino gain (Documentary Fact). (5) Structure: two debt groups, secured debt ahead of USD 1,133.4 million of unsecured notes, floating-rate term loans of USD 2,542.5 million at effective rates between 8.86% and 9.38% (Documentary Fact). (6) Concentration: the U.S. Government at 16% and the five largest contracts at 19% (Documentary Fact), with termination-for-convenience rights described by management (Management Language, qualified). (7) Visibility gaps: no company-defined EBITDA, covenant levels or group-level financials (Insufficient Information; missing evidence is not read as adverse).
